Landing Pages and Ad Review: Why Yours Gets Rejected

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 2 June 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the ad platform before the visitor sees it. Reviewers check that the page matches the ad, works, identifies the business, carries the disclosures the category requires and makes no claims it cannot support; Google publishes most of these checks in its destination, misrepresentation and financial services policies. To pass and convert, match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the visitor's doubts, and never show reviewers and users different pages.

A landing page is the page a visitor arrives at from a particular source: an ad, a creator's link, an affiliate placement, an email. It exists to do one thing, and it is reviewed by two audiences before it does it: the platform's reviewer, and the person who arrives.

For companies in reviewed categories, the first audience is where most landing pages fail.

What a landing page is for

One source, one message, one action. A visitor who clicked an ad about a savings account should land on a page about that account, not on the homepage. The page should confirm they are in the right place, state the offer, answer the two or three doubts that stop people, provide proof, and ask for a single action. Everything else is a distraction, and on a page with a specific job, distraction is measured in lost conversions.

The same logic sits behind content with a job: a named reader, a decision, a next action. A landing page is the shortest piece of content a company writes, and the one with the most precise job.

How ad platforms review it

Every major platform reviews the landing page as well as the ad, and rejects the pair if the page violates policy. Google's published rules are the most detailed, and they describe what other platforms check in similar terms.

What reviewers checkWhere Google says itWhat the page needs
The page works and can be crawledDestination requirements: pages that "don't function properly", return errors to Google's crawler, or are not crawlable are disapprovedA live, fast page that loads for the crawler and in every targeted location
The ad and page matchDestination requirements on mismatched domains and redirects; misrepresentation rules on "unclear relevance" and "unavailable offers"The offer in the ad, findable on the page, on the same domain
Real content, not a shellDestination requirements on pages "designed for the primary purpose of showing ads" or with insufficient original contentA complete page with original material
Who is behind itMisrepresentation rules on "obscuring, or omitting material information about your identity"Legal name, address, contact and registration details
What it costsMisrepresentation rules on failing to disclose "the payment model or full expense"Fees and pricing stated plainly
Category disclosuresFinancial services policy: physical address, fees and accreditation links, visible immediatelyRequired disclaimers, licences and registration numbers on the page itself
ClaimsMisrepresentation rules on "unreliable claims" that promise "an improbable result", and on clickbaitClaims the company can evidence, with no manufactured urgency
Same page for everyoneCircumventing systems policy on cloakingOne page, shown identically to reviewers and users

Google policies checked on 16 November 2026.

Pages fail review most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, and category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy. The financial services rule is stricter than many teams realise: Google says disclosures "can't be posted as roll-over text or made available through another link or tab". A fee table in a collapsed accordion can fail on that alone.

Other platforms push the same disclosures onto the page. TikTok's financial services policy requires advertisers of loans and credit cards in several European markets to disclose rates, fees and repayment terms on their landing pages.

Why restricted-category pages get rejected

The categories the platforms review (financial products, crypto, health, supplements, gambling, dating) are reviewed against stricter claim rules, and the page is often what triggers the classification. A page that mentions yield, returns, weight or winnings is sorted into the category by its vocabulary before a human reads it. Google's healthcare policy states this directly for drugs: it restricts the use of prescription-drug terms "in ads, landing pages, and keywords".

That is worth knowing, but it is not an invitation to disguise the page. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or route reviewers differently from users are the fastest way to a permanent account ban and, in regulated categories, to a regulator's attention. Google's circumventing systems policy treats cloaking as egregious: the account is suspended upon detection, without prior warning, and the advertiser cannot advertise with Google Ads again.

A page in a restricted category should be visibly and compliantly in that category, with the licences, disclaimers and disclosures the platform requires, and the company should know from its band map whether that platform will run it at all. Our explainer on what a restricted category is covers the map.

A page in a restricted category should be visibly and compliantly in that category.

What a page that passes and converts contains

ElementWhy it is there
A headline that repeats the promise the visitor clicked on, in their wordsConfirms they are in the right place; satisfies the match check
One or two sentences on what changes for themStates the offer without inflating it
The action, visible without scrolling, with a label that says what happens nextOne page, one action
The two or three most common doubts answered briefly: is my money safe, what does it cost, how long does it takeRemoves the questions that stop people
Proof matched to those doubts: the custodian, the licence, the review, the numberTurns claims into evidence
Business identity in the footer: legal name, address, contact, registrationSatisfies identity and category disclosure rules
Required disclaimers and a privacy policy, linked, with category disclosures on the page itselfMeets the "visible immediately" standard where it applies
Speed on mobileMost reviewed-category traffic is mobile

Nothing else. Each extra element is a new place for a claim to go wrong and a new distraction from the action. Test changes one at a time against a decision written in advance; campaign testing that reaches a decision covers how.

For channels other than ads

Affiliate, creator and email traffic lands too, and those pages are not reviewed by a platform, which tempts companies to relax. Do not. The compliance library that governs the ads should govern every page, because regulators read landing pages and creators send their audiences there.

The regulators' standard does not depend on the channel. The UK Financial Conduct Authority requires cryptoasset promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading, with specific risk warnings and a 24-hour cooling-off period for first-time investors, whatever route the visitor took. The US Federal Trade Commission's 2023 Endorsement Guides set out the potential liability of advertisers, not only endorsers, for what is said on their behalf. A partner page with a loose claim is still the company's claim. Referral partners without leakage covers how to brief partners so their pages stay inside the claims library.

And every page should ask for an email address before or after the main action, because the visitor arrived through a rented channel and the company should leave with something it owns.

A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the platform before the visitor sees it. Match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the doubts, and never build a page designed to be read differently by reviewers and users.

lowob takeaways

  • Write the page for the reviewer first. Working, crawlable, matched to the ad, with real content.
  • Put identity and fees on the page. Google's financial rules require them visible immediately.
  • Expect vocabulary to trigger review. Yield, returns and drug terms sort a page into its category.
  • Never cloak. One page for reviewers and users, or a permanent ban.
  • Apply the same library to partner pages. Regulators read them, and advertisers carry liability.

Common questions

Why does my landing page keep getting rejected by ad platforms?

Most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, or category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy. Reviewers also check that the page works, can be crawled, matches the ad, carries required disclaimers and avoids fake urgency.

What does Google require on a financial services landing page?

The physical address of the business, associated fees and links to any claimed accreditation, visible immediately rather than in roll-over text or behind another link or tab, plus loan terms such as maximum APR for personal loans.

Can I hide that my landing page is about crypto or finance to pass ad review?

No. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or show reviewers something different from users are treated as circumventing systems, which Google punishes with suspension on detection and no right to advertise again.

What should a high-converting landing page contain?

A headline repeating the promise the visitor clicked on, a line on what changes for them, a visible action, brief answers to the two or three most common doubts with matching proof, business identity in the footer, required disclaimers, and fast mobile load.
